Beat generation. A literary and cultural movement of the nineteen fifties and nineteen sixties, centered on American poets and writers who rejected conformity and materialism and Cold War militarism. Beat writers pioneered spontaneous composition and championed Eastern philosophy and celebrated sexuality and drug use, adopting a countercultural stance that influenced rock music and youth rebellion and the broader counterculture of the nineteen sixties. Figures like Allen Ginsberg and Jack Kerouac and Lawrence Ferlinghetti redefined what American literature could be and what poets could address.

The Beats rejected the formalism and established literary institutions of their era, favoring raw emotional expression and spontaneous composition and oral performance over polished formal verse and academic poetics. Allen Ginsberg's poem Howl from nineteen fifty-six became the iconic Beat text, featuring long lines and prophetic rage and explicit sexual and spiritual content that shocked the literary establishment and sparked obscenity trials. Jack Kerouac's On the Road from nineteen fifty-seven captured Beat restlessness and spontaneity, defining a generation's appetite for travel and experience and liberation from suburban conformity and institutional constraints.

The movement drew heavily on Zen Buddhism and Eastern philosophy, seeing spiritual search and enlightenment as central to the poet's mission and life, not just literary technique. Beatniks, the stereotypical Beat figures with goatees and berets and bongo drums in coffeehouses, emerged partly as media caricature that both misrepresented and popularized a more serious literary movement. The Beats were direct forerunners of the nineteen sixties counterculture and youth rebellion, anticipating its rejection of authority and drug experimentation and sexual liberation and passionate anti-war political activism.

Beat writers valued authenticity and immediacy and confession, seeing the personal voice and lived experience as more truthful and urgent than literary polish or academic detachment from the world. The Beats' embrace of jazz rhythm and bebop language influenced American poetry's adoption of oral and vernacular styles, breaking away from previous generations' formal poetic diction and constraints. Allen Ginsberg was a central figure of the movement and author of Howl, the Beat manifesto. American poetry is the tradition the Beats revolutionized through spontaneity and demotic language. Counterculture is the broader movement of rebellion and dissent the Beats helped catalyze. The Vietnam War was the political cause that energized Beat and broader antiwar sentiment. Rebellion and dissent is the fundamental stance against conformity that defined the generation.
